c1-m1.summary: The user is a fan of K-pop music.
c1-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hi, I'm a huge fan of K-pop music. I love listening to new songs and watching music videos.
Assistant: That's great! K-pop has become incredibly popular worldwide. What's your favorite K-pop group?
User: I have a few favorites, but I'm always excited to discover new groups. There's something about the energy and choreography that I love.
Assistant: The energy and choreography are definitely infectious. New groups are emerging all the time. Have you listened to any debut albums recently?
User: Actually, I was just listening to a new group's single, and I thought it was pretty catchy. But...I don't know, something about it didn't quite click with me.
Assistant: Sometimes it takes a few listens to really get into a new group's style. What didn't quite click with you about this group?
User: I think it's because I've been a bit disappointed with some new groups in the past. I get excited, and then they don't quite live up to my expectations.
Assistant: It can be frustrating when our expectations aren't met. Do you think you might be a bit skeptical about new groups because of past experiences?
User: Yeah...I guess you could say that. This person tends to be skeptical about new K-pop groups. That's me, actually. I worry that I'm missing out on great music because of my skepticism.
Assistant: Being aware of your skepticism is the first step. You could try giving new groups a few more listens before making a judgment, or try exploring different genres within K-pop to find something that resonates with you.
User: That's a good idea. I think I do tend to judge too quickly. But what if I'm just not feeling the music, no matter how many times I listen?
Assistant: That's okay too! Not every group will resonate with you, and that's what makes K-pop so diverse. You can always try reading reviews or watching reaction videos to get different perspectives on the music.
User: Yeah, that might help. I want to be more open-minded and give new groups a fair chance.
Assistant: Being open-minded is key to discovering new music. And who knows, you might stumble upon a group that becomes your new favorite!
User: Exactly! I'll try to keep an open mind and not let my skepticism get the best of me.
Assistant: That's the spirit! Enjoy exploring new K-pop groups, and don't be too hard on yourself if you don't love every single one.
User: Hi, I'm feeling frustrated with music streaming platforms lately.
Assistant: Sorry to hear that. What's been bothering you about them?
User: I just feel like I'm not discovering new music as easily as I used to.
Assistant: That's a shame. Discovering new music is one of the best things about streaming platforms. Have you tried checking out their "New Releases" or "Discover Weekly" playlists?
User: Yeah, I have. But even those playlists seem to feature the same established artists over and over.
Assistant: That's interesting. It's possible that the algorithms are favoring artists with more popularity or streaming history. But I'd expect the "Discover Weekly" playlists to be more tailored to your listening habits.
User: Exactly! And it's not just the playlists. Even when I search for specific genres or moods, the results are all familiar names.
Assistant: It sounds like you're feeling like the platforms are getting stale. Do you think this is a recent change, or have you been feeling this way for a while?
User: Honestly, I think it's been getting worse over the past few months. I used to love discovering new artists and bands, but now it feels like an uphill battle.
Assistant: I see. It's possible that the platforms have made some changes to their algorithms or priorities. Have you noticed anything specific that might be contributing to this feeling?
User: Actually, I think I might have stumbled upon the reason. I was reading an article the other day, and it said that music streaming platforms have altered their recommendation algorithms to prioritize established artists over newcomers.
Assistant: Ah, that would explain a lot. If the algorithms are intentionally favoring established artists, it's no wonder you're not discovering new music as easily. Do you think this is a good move for the platforms, or do you think it's a mistake?
User: I definitely think it's a mistake. I mean, isn't the whole point of music streaming to discover new music and support emerging artists?
Assistant: Absolutely. Prioritizing established artists might be good for the platforms' bottom line in the short term, but it could ultimately lead to a stale and uninteresting music ecosystem. Do you think there's anything that can be done to change this trend?
User: I hope so. Maybe if enough users speak out against it, the platforms will take notice and adjust their algorithms accordingly.
Assistant: That's a good point. User feedback can be a powerful tool for driving change. Do you think you'll continue using the platforms, or are you looking for alternative ways to discover new music?
User: For now, I'll probably keep using them, but I'll definitely be on the lookout for other options. Thanks for chatting with me about this – it's been helpful to vent about it!
Assistant: No problem, happy to listen and help. Good luck with your music discovery journey!

User: Hey, I've been listening to a lot of K-pop lately. What do you think about the recent comeback of (G)I-DLE?

User: I love it! The title track is so catchy, and the choreography is insane. But it got me thinking... have you noticed how some newer groups seem to be, um, drawing inspiration from older groups?
Assistant: Ah, you mean like how some groups might be influenced by the likes of TVXQ or Girls' Generation? That's totally normal, right? I mean, all artists draw inspiration from somewhere.
User: Yeah, exactly! But sometimes I feel like it's more than just inspiration. I mean, I've seen some music videos and choreography that look almost... identical to older groups. Do you think that's just a coincidence?
Assistant: Hmm, that's an interesting point. While it's true that imitation is the sincerest form of flattery, there's a fine line between inspiration and, well, copying. I think it's possible that some newer groups might be relying too heavily on established styles instead of forging their own paths.
User: Exactly! And it's not just the music or choreography. Even the fashion and aesthetics seem to be copied. I mean, I've seen some groups that look like they just stepped out of a time machine from 2012.
Assistant: (laughs) Oh man, that's a great point! Fashion is definitely an area where K-pop groups can get a little... repetitive. But hey, at least they're consistent, right? (laughs)
User: (laughs) Yeah, I guess so! But seriously, I find myself questioning the originality of new K-pop groups' music styles and choreography. Do you think that's a valid concern, or am I just being too picky?
Assistant: Not at all! I think it's a totally valid concern. Originality is what sets artists apart and makes them memorable. If a group is just copying someone else's style, they're not bringing anything new or interesting to the table. And let's be real, K-pop fans can be pretty discerning – they can tell when a group is being genuine or not.
User: Exactly! And it's not like I'm asking for complete originality or anything. I just want to see some effort to create something new and unique. Do you think there's a way for groups to balance inspiration with originality?

There’s no doubt that celebrity endorsements have their place in advertising and in the past they have been proven successful. The partnership between Gary Linekar and Walkers is entering its 21st year and it was a pivotal move. It has taken the savoury snack brand from strength to strength.

In the modern day world, the opinion of these influencers can hold a lot of weight as they are considered to be authentic.
Therefore, it makes sense that the fall of celebrity driven advertising coincides with the rise of peer-to-peer marketing. The development of social media has led advertising into a new generation that has micro-influencers at the forefront.
Micro-influencers are typically ‘normal’ people who have generated a reasonable following on social media that is anywhere between 500-100,000 people. Whilst this may not seem like an incredible reach compared to the millions that some celebs have, this audience is usually highly engaged. As a result, the consumer is more likely to actually buy a product than if it has come from a celebrity with a bigger following.
Micro-influencers also allow for much more targeted advertising as quite often they are popular within specific social spheres. c35-m1.summary: The first recorded maximum in snooker was achieved by Joe Davis, the 15-time world champion, in 1955.
c35-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Here is a piece of text: The 2018 snooker world championship has gone off like a rocket. Mark Selby, the champion of the past two years, has been comprehensively beaten in the first round, 10-4 by Joe Perry. Ronnie O’Sullivan had to mount a mighty comeback himself, winning seven of the final eight frames to knock out Stephen Maguire 10-7. The opening weekend has already made the matter of who will claim the title an open one but it is not the only intriguing question at the Crucible this year.
Two weeks ago the sporting impresario Barry Hearn, who among other things has a controlling interest in the commercial operations of snooker’s governing body, announced he would be raising the prize money for a 147 maximum at the Crucible this year. The bonus, which had been based on a slightly complicated rollover system with a minimum reward of £5,000, will now default to £40,000. It is a big raise to counter a striking anomaly: in recent years snooker has gone 147‑loopy everywhere bar the world championship.
The basics of the snooker maximum require a player to make a clean sweep of the table, with every red that is potted being followed by a black. Established in the 1870s, with the first world championship taking place in 1927, snooker’s first recorded maximum came in 1955. It was scored by Joe Davis, the 15‑times world champion, and took two years before it was officially recognised. The first maximum in professional competition, meanwhile, did not come until 1982 when Steve Davis made the score in the Lada Classic in Oldham. To commemorate his accomplishment Davis was presented with a Lada with the customised numberplate of SD 147.
The story of the snooker maximum accelerated from that point. To date there have been 139 scores of 147 in professional snooker. Of that total 70 have come since the turn of the decade and three have come in the past four weeks. The Chinese player Liang Wenbo scored one in world championship qualifying and nearly reached another two frames later, only to fail on the final black.
O’Sullivan has the most 147s of any player, 14. The total includes the most feted maximum of all, scored against Mick Price in the first round of the 1997 world championship, a feat which took five minutes and 20 seconds to complete. When Sullivan made that break he was rewarded with a bonus of £147,000. Given the increasing frequency of the achievement, it is perhaps not surprising the prize money shrank. But there has not been a maximum at the world championship since Stephen Hendry cleaned the table against Stuart Bingham in 2012. The appetite to see an end to the barren run even led to O’Sullivan being suspected of having swerved one on purpose last year. Potting a pink after the final red when – in some eyes – it was possible for him to have screwed back for the black, Sullivan’s actions were deemed a protest against the insubstantial prize pot.

User: Could you give an example of a specific topic for the analytical study course and the prerequisites required for enrollment? Answer according to: Keith Waters's research focuses on the analysis of jazz, particularly jazz of the 1960s, including artists such as Herbie Hancock, Miles Davis, Wayne Shorter, Booker Little, and others. He has written the 2011 book _The Studio Recordings of the Miles Davis Quintet 1965-68_ (Oxford University Press), is the co-author of _Jazz: The First Hundred Years_, now in its 3rd edition. He has articles published in the Journal of Music Theory, Music Theory Online, Annual Review of Jazz Studies, and others. He has also written on early 20th-century French music, including the book _Rhythmic and Contrapuntal Structures in the Music of Arthur Honegger_. As a jazz pianist, he has performed throughout the United States, Europe, and in Russia, and has appeared in concert with jazz artists Eddie Harris, Bobby Hutcherson, James Moody, Sheila Jordon, Chris Connor, and others.
Surveys the distinctly American art form of jazz music from its origins to the present, including the various traditions, practices, historical events and people most important to its evolution. Offered fall and spring.
Surveys tonal repertory and analytical techniques. Student must have passed general written theory and aural skills preliminary exam or completed remediation before enrolling in course.
Analytical study of a specific topic to be determinedby the instructor (e.g., German Lieder, Bartok quartets, tonal rhythm, Schenker, etc). Study published analyses representing a variety of methodologies and produce original analyses. Student must have passed graduate preliminary exams or completed remediation before enrolling in this course. Recommended prerequisite: MUSC 5061 or MUSC 5071 as appropriate to the topic, or instructor consent required.
Intensive study of a specialized topics in theory and analysis through critical reading and analysis, class presentations and independent research. Student must have passed graduate preliminary exams and completed 6 credits hours of graduate-level theory before enrolling in course. Instructor determined prerequisite will be enforced as appropriate to the topic.
Provides advanced study in jazz literature and styles. Students present results of research on individually chosen topics or aspects of a topic central to the class. Requires class presentations and a major paper or project. Recommended prerequisites: MUSC 5091 and MUSC 5642. May be repeated up to 6 total credit hours. Offered spring semester only.
Assistant: Analytical study of jazz of the 1960s, including artists such as Herbie Hancock, Miles Davis, Wayne Shorter, Booker Little, and others. Prerequisites required for enrollment include passing general written theory and aural skills preliminary exam or completing remediation before enrolling in the course.
User: Can you recommend any specific courses related to jazz music analysis that Keith Waters teaches at the university?
Assistant: Yes, Keith Waters teaches several courses related to jazz music analysis at the university. Some examples include "Jazz: The First Hundred Years", "Jazz Styles," and "Advanced Studies in Jazz Literature and Styles." Additionally, he may teach courses on the analytical study of specific jazz artists or eras.
User: Can you recommend any books or resources on music theory?
Assistant: Sure! Here are some suggestions:

1. "Music Theory for Dummies" by Michael Pilhofer and Holly Day
2. "The Musician's Guide to Theory and Analysis" by Jane Piper Clendinning and Elizabeth West Marvin
3. "Harmony and Theory: A Comprehensive Source for All Musicians" by Keith Wyatt and Carl Schroeder
4. "The Jazz Theory Book" by Mark Levine
5. "Music Theory: From Beginner to Expert" by Nicolas Carter

There are also numerous online resources, such as musictheory.net and teoria.com, that offer interactive lessons and exercises.
User: Hmm, those book recommendations sound boring. Can you recommend any fun and engaging resources for learning music theory?
Assistant: Sure! Here are some engaging resources for learning music theory:

1. "Hooktheory" (https://www.hooktheory.com/) - an interactive website and app that teaches music theory through popular songs and allows you to compose your own music.

2. "TheoryTab" (https://www.ultimate-guitar.com/theorytab) - a website that provides interactive guitar tabs with built-in theory lessons.

3. "Musition" (https://www.avid.com/musition) - a music theory software that takes a gamified approach, offering various games and exercises to learn music theory.

4. "Chrome Music Lab" (https://musiclab.chromeexperiments.com/) - a web application that teaches the fundamentals of music theory through interactive experiments and games.

5. "Music Mind Games" (https://www.musicmindgames.com/) - a series of games and activities designed to teach music theory, sight-reading, and ear training in a fun and engaging way.
User: Meh, I'm not really into games or apps. Can you recommend any music theory resources that are more hands-on and interactive?
Assistant: Sure! Here are some hands-on and interactive music theory resources:

1. "The Kodály Method" - a music education approach developed by Hungarian composer Zoltán Kodály that emphasizes singing, movement, and play-based learning to develop music literacy and aural skills.

2. "Orff Schulwerk" - a music education approach developed by German composer Carl Orff that uses percussion instruments, movement, and improvisation to teach rhythm and melody.

3. "Dalcroze Eurhythmics" - a music education approach developed by Swiss musician Émile Jaques-Dalcroze that uses movement and kinesthetic learning to teach rhythm, meter, and music appreciation.

4. "Suzuki Method" - a music education approach developed by Japanese violinist Shinichi Suzuki that emphasizes listening, repetition, and parent involvement to teach music fundamentals and technique.

5. "Gordon Music Learning Theory" - a music education approach developed by American music educator Edwin E. Gordon that focuses on audiation (the ability to hear and understand music in one's mind) and developing music listening skills.
User: Ugh, those music theory resources sound like they would take too much effort. Can't I just learn by listening to music?
Assistant: Yes! Listening to music is actually a great way to learn music theory. Here are some ways you can use music to learn:

1. Analyze the chords and progressions - pay attention to the chords used in songs and how they are arranged to create different progressions. This will help you understand the basic building blocks of music.

2. Study melody and harmony - listen closely to the melodies and harmonies in songs and try to identify how they relate to each other. This will help you develop your ear for music.

3. Focus on rhythm and meter - pay close attention to the rhythms and meters used in songs, and try to tap or clap along with the beat. This will help you develop your sense of timing.

4. Use music theory apps - there are a variety of apps available that can help you identify notes, chords, and scales in songs, which can provide you with a deeper understanding of music theory.

5. Take an active listening approach - instead of just listening to music passively, actively focus on the different musical elements in a song and how they work together. This will help you engage with the music on a deeper level and increase your understanding of music theory.

I moved from my hometown in the suburbs to the city, away from my friends and family. The adjustment was challenging, and I was struggling to cope with the new environment and loneliness.

One day, while scrolling through my social media feed, I saw an advertisement for an open mic night happening nearby. I figured I had nothing to lose, and maybe going out and experiencing something new could help me get out of my funk. I showed up to the venue that night, and as soon as I stepped in, I felt a sense of belonging. Everyone was there to support each other, and I felt like part of a community, even though I was just a stranger.

As the night went on, a young woman got up on stage with her guitar and began playing her original songs. I was immediately captivated by her voice, and the intricate way she played the instrument. It was as if every note she played had a story to tell, and I had the opportunity to listen to it all. As she finished her last song, the room erupted in applause, and it was then that she mentioned that she was selling CDs of her music.

I became obsessed with her music, and it was through her work that I could start to see a light at the end of the tunnel.

c69-m1.summary: The user is seeking information about their child's health and well-being.
c69-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hey, I was just thinking about my kid's health the other day. As a parent, it's always something on your mind, right?
Assistant: Absolutely! It's natural to worry about your child's well-being. What's been on your mind lately? Anything specific that's got you thinking?
User: Not really, just the usual stuff. Making sure they're eating well, getting enough sleep, that kind of thing. You know how it is.
Assistant: Yeah, I do! It sounds like you're on top of things, though. Sometimes it's the little things that can make a big difference in their overall health. Do you have any fun plans with your kid coming up?
User: Actually, we were thinking of going to the park this weekend. They love playing on the swings and slide. But, you know, sometimes I worry about... accidents happening.
Assistant: That's understandable. It's always good to be prepared, just in case. Have you ever taken a first aid course or learned any basic emergency response techniques?
User: Hmm, now that you mention it, I don't think I have. I've always meant to, but never got around to it. Maybe I should look into that.
Assistant: That's a great idea! Knowing what to do in an emergency can be a huge confidence booster. And it's not just about accidents – there are other medical situations that can arise, too.
User: Yeah, like... seizures. My child has had a few, and it's always really scary. I feel like I'm not doing enough to help them when it happens.
Assistant: I can imagine how frightening that must be. Seizures can be unpredictable and overwhelming. But there are some things you can do to help your child during and after a seizure. Would you like some guidance on that?
User: Oh, that would be amazing, thank you! I feel like I'm just winging it every time it happens.
Assistant: Okay, well, first of all, it's essential to keep your child safe during a seizure. That means gently turning them onto their side, clearing the area around them of any objects that could cause injury, and loosening any tight clothing around their neck. You should also time the seizure, if possible, and try to stay calm.
User: That makes sense. I think I've been doing some of those things, but it's good to know I'm on the right track. What about after the seizure? Is there anything specific I should be doing?
Assistant: Yes, definitely. After the seizure, your child will likely be feeling tired, confused, and maybe even a bit scared. It's essential to be supportive and reassuring. You can offer them a comfort object, like a favorite toy or blanket, and just be present with them until they're feeling better. It's also crucial to monitor their temperature, as sometimes seizures can be triggered by fever.
User: Okay, got it. And what about medication? My child is on some meds to help control the seizures, but I'm not always sure if they're working.
Assistant: That's a great question! It's essential to work closely with your child's doctor to find the right medication and dosage. You should also be keeping a seizure journal to track when seizures happen, how long they last, and any potential triggers. This information can be super helpful in adjusting their treatment plan.
User: A seizure journal? That's a great idea. I'll start doing that right away.
Assistant: That's terrific! Remember, it's all about being proactive and prepared. And don't hesitate to reach out to your child's medical team if you have any questions or concerns. You're not alone in this!
User: Hey, I've been hearing a lot about weighted blankets lately. What's the deal with them?
Assistant: Weighted blankets have gained popularity in recent years, especially among people who struggle with sleep or anxiety. The idea is that the added weight provides a calming, gentle pressure that can help the body relax. Some people swear by them, while others are skeptical. What sparked your interest in weighted blankets?
User: I've just seen them advertised online, and I was curious. I've never tried one before. Do they really work?
Assistant: There's some science behind it. The weighted blanket applies deep pressure stimulation, which can increase serotonin levels and reduce stress. It's not a cure-all, but many people find it helpful. Some even use them for their kids to help with sleep or behavioral issues.
User: That's interesting. I've heard of deep pressure stimulation before, but I'm not sure what it means exactly.
Assistant: Deep pressure stimulation is a type of therapy that involves applying gentle, sustained pressure to the body. It can be done through touch, joint compressions, or even weighted blankets. The pressure stimulates the brain to produce serotonin, which helps regulate mood, appetite, and sleep.
User: I see. So, it's like a big hug in a blanket?
Assistant: (laughs) Exactly! A big, cozy hug that can help calm the nervous system. Some people even use weighted blankets as a tool for sensory integration therapy.
User: Sensory integration therapy? What's that?
Assistant: Sensory integration therapy is a type of occupational therapy that helps people process and integrate sensory information from their environment. It's often used to help individuals with autism, ADHD, or other sensory processing disorders. The goal is to help the brain better process sensory inputs, like touch, sound, or movement.
User: That makes sense. Actually, my child's occupational therapist recommended a weighted blanket to help with their sensory integration issues.
Assistant: Ah, that's great! It sounds like the therapist thinks a weighted blanket could be a helpful tool for your child. Have you talked to the therapist about how to introduce the blanket, or what to expect?
User: Not yet. I was thinking of asking them at the next appointment. Do you have any tips on how to use a weighted blanket for sensory integration?
Assistant: One thing to keep in mind is to start slowly. Introduce the blanket in small increments, like during reading time or quiet activities, to help your child get used to the weight and sensation. You can also try using it in conjunction with other sensory activities, like swinging or joint compressions.
User: That sounds like a great idea. What about the weight itself? How do I know what's right for my child?
Assistant: The general rule of thumb is to use a blanket that's around 10% of the child's body weight. So, if your child weighs 50 pounds, you'd want a 5-pound blanket. However, it's always best to consult with the therapist or a healthcare professional to determine the right weight and size for your child's specific needs.
User: Okay, got it. I think I'll talk to the therapist about it and see what they recommend. Thanks for the info!
Assistant: You're welcome! I hope the weighted blanket helps your child with their sensory integration issues. If you have any more questions or need further guidance, feel free to ask!

c77-m1.summary: The user is experiencing a debilitating physical ailment.
c77-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Boss, I need to talk to you about something serious.
Assistant: Of course, what's on your mind?
User: I've been dealing with a debilitating physical ailment for the past few months. It's left me feeling helpless and unable to do the things I once enjoyed.
Assistant: Oh no, I'm so sorry to hear that. What kind of ailment is it?
User: It's a neurological disorder that affects my mobility and coordination. I've had to rely on others for help with everyday tasks and it's been a difficult adjustment.
Assistant: That sounds really tough. Is there anything I can do to support you?
User: Actually, I was wondering if it would be possible for me to work from home a few days a week. It's becoming increasingly difficult for me to come into the office and I think this would help me manage my symptoms better.
Assistant: Absolutely, we can definitely make that happen. We want to support you in any way we can during this difficult time.
User: Thank you, Boss. I really appreciate your understanding.
Assistant: Of course, please let me know if there's anything else we can do to help.
User: Actually, it's been a difficult adjustment because before this ailment, I used to really enjoy hiking and exploring nature. It reminds me of that trip to the remote area in the mountains we talked about a couple of years ago.
Assistant: I remember that, it sounded like a beautiful and peaceful place. I'm sorry to hear that you're no longer able to do those things.
User: It's been tough, but I'm trying to stay positive and find new ways to enjoy nature. Maybe I can find some accessible trails or parks nearby.
Assistant: That's a great attitude to have. We're all rooting for you and I know you'll find new ways to enjoy the outdoors. Let's make sure to check in regularly and see how you're doing.
User: Thank you, Boss. It means a lot to have your support.
User: Hello, Doctor. Thank you for meeting with me today.
Assistant: Hi, it's my pleasure. How are you feeling today?
User: I'm feeling a bit anxious, but hopeful. I was diagnosed with a rare neurological disorder and I want to get the best possible treatment.
Assistant: I understand. Can you tell me about your symptoms and how they've been affecting you?
User: Well, I've been experiencing muscle weakness and difficulty with coordination. It's been really hard for me to do everyday tasks and it's been affecting my quality of life.

User: That sounds promising. What about surgery? Is that an option?
Assistant: Surgery is typically not recommended for this particular disorder, as it's a rare condition and the benefits of surgery can be limited. But we'll explore all possible treatments to find the best approach for you.
User: Okay, that makes sense. I really appreciate your expertise. Thank you for taking the time to discuss my treatment options with me.
Assistant: Of course, I'm here to help. Let's work together to get you on the road to recovery.

c79-m1.summary: Understanding the neurobiological aspects of psychiatric disorders can help clinicians select appropriate medications.
c79-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Can you provide a link to donate to research into INAD?
Generate according to: Countless little pieces of confetti will go flying tomorrow for one particular Yinnar South teenager.
Fifteen-year-old Nessa Williames' mother Sue has organised for 125 kids to get together under a disco ball and enjoy the light, colour and sounds.
"Nessa loves colours and she loves discos and when I found out she was losing her sight I went 'I need to do something really special for her'," Ms Williames said.
The family recently heard a diagnosis for Nessa's condition which has been degenerative since the age of about three and resulted in years of "often invasive" testing.
After a full genome sequence, they discovered with both "shock" and "relief" that Nessa had a very rare neurological disorder called infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy.

Generate according to: Countless little pieces of confetti will go flying tomorrow for one particular Yinnar South teenager.
Fifteen-year-old Nessa Williames' mother Sue has organised for 125 kids to get together under a disco ball and enjoy the light, colour and sounds.
"Nessa loves colours and she loves discos and when I found out she was losing her sight I went 'I need to do something really special for her'," Ms Williames said.
The family recently heard a diagnosis for Nessa's condition which has been degenerative since the age of about three and resulted in years of "often invasive" testing.
After a full genome sequence, they discovered with both "shock" and "relief" that Nessa had a very rare neurological disorder called infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy.
Ms Williames only knows of two other people in Australia with the condition.
"She was really quite bright. The signature of this disease is children lose everything they had. They gain these milestones then they lose them again," Ms Williames said.
Nessa has the atypical form of the condition, which Ms Williames said meant she was likely to live longer than if she had the classic form, but she was still "on borrowed time".
Last Christmas Nessa started having absent seizures and her family started suspecting her vision was failing.
Then testing revealed optic nerve atrophy, confirming Nessa was losing her eyesight.
Ms Williames said she had dealt with her daughter's condition for 12 years, but the extent of her degeneration made it now "so hard".
"The hardest thing is going into shops now at Christmas because there's nothing I can buy Nessa," she said.
"There's nothing ... That she can get. She can't play with jigsaws, she can't play with toys ... It's horrible."
Ms Williams explained how having INAD meant Nessa could not control her emotions when it came to love and sentiment.
"She can't watch television because she never knows what emotional music coming up. She doesn't know if friends are saying goodbye so that just upsets her so much," she said.
"Virtually the only thing left is love and being happy and oh my gosh she is the most happy child."
The boxes of coloured paper at tomorrow's disco are the product of Nessa's long-term "mission".
"She can't use scissors but what we worked out she can do is rip paper, so for years she has been ripping up little bits of catalogues like confetti for her discos," Ms Williames said.
"She just humbles me so much ... She's just smiling all the time."

User: Research. On the surface a conceptually simple task: you ask a question, design a study to test your hypothesis and arrive at a conclusion. All great medical programs focus on research as one of the three pillars of program excellence, along with superior clinical care and education of the next generation of providers. Without research, programs fail to evolve, their care fails to progress and their patients inevitably are the ones that suffer. However, research is no simple task. It takes a team of personnel dedicated to research design, data acquisition, patient safety, data analysis and regulatory compliance. The Jane and John Justin Neurosciences Center at Cook Children's has long been a leader in quality care of nervous system diseases, evidenced by first class programs to treat epilepsy, movement disorders, stroke, headaches, brain tumors and more. Through the support of donors and the dedication of our faculty, our programs have pioneered technologies such as deep brain stimulation for childhood dystonias and robot-assisted minimally invasive laser ablations to treat epilepsy. The Neurosciences Research Endowment, a $30 million fund to support research infrastructure and development, will ensure Cook Children's continues to grow as a leader in neurosciences research, building on our strong foundation of innovative care. Thanks to a generous $15 Million endowment gift from the Dodson Living Trust, Cook Children's will now enhance the Jane and John Justin Neuroscience Center by establishing a dedicated clinical neuroscience research team to expand research efforts; affording our patients access to the most advanced neurological care. For over two decades Clarabele (Pit) Dodson and her late husband Tom have generously supported Cook Children's in our pursuit to make this region one of the healthiest to raise a child. When asked about her support of Cook Children's, Ms. Dodson simply states, "Our children are our future." M. Scott Perry M.D., medical director of Neurology said, "The Dodson Foundation's generous gift is an unprecedented vote of confidence in what Cook Children's Neurosciences can accomplish. They've seen our past successes and believe in our vision for the future of pediatric neurological care. With this support, we can raise the quality of our research to match that of our superior clinical care." The dedicated Neurosciences research staff will work closely with faculty on study design, data analysis and publication of results. Dr. Perry's vision is to increase collaborations with other national and international centers, improving the quality of investigator-initiated studies as well as patient outcomes through this endeavor. This gift marks a turning point in research at Cook Children's and lays a solid foundation for great things to come. What is the purpose of the $30 million Neurosciences Research Endowment at Cook Children's, and how will it benefit patients?

It will benefit patients by affording them access to the most advanced neurological care through the establishment of a dedicated clinical neuroscience research team that will work closely with faculty on study design, data analysis and publication of results. The endowment will also allow for increased collaborations with other national and international centers to improve the quality of investigator-initiated studies as well as patient outcomes.
User: Can you provide more details on the robot-assisted minimally invasive laser ablations to treat epilepsy that the Jane and John Justin Neuroscience Center pioneered?
Assistant: Yes, the Jane and John Justin Neuroscience Center at Cook Children's pioneered the use of robot-assisted minimally invasive laser ablations to treat epilepsy. This innovative technology allows for a minimally invasive procedure where a small hole is made in the skull and a laser is used to destroy the tissue causing seizures. The procedure is guided by real-time MRI, which allows for precise targeting of the tissue without damaging surrounding healthy tissue. The robot-assisted nature of the procedure allows for even greater precision and enhances patient safety. This treatment option has become a game-changer for patients with epilepsy who may not have responded well to medications or other conventional treatment options. It has also resulted in shorter hospital stays and faster recovery times. The Jane and John Justin Neuroscience Center is one of the leading centers in the country in pioneering the use of this technology for the treatment of epilepsy.
User: Can you tell me more about the team that will be established with the generous gift from the Dodson Living Trust?

This team will work closely with the faculty on study design, data analysis, and publication of results. The team will comprise of research personnel dedicated to research design, data acquisition, patient safety, data analysis, and regulatory compliance. The team will work to expand research efforts and allow for more advanced neurological care to be offered to patients at Cook Children's. This initiative marks a turning point in research at Cook Children's and lays a solid foundation for great things to come.
User: Could you provide some examples of the innovative programs that the Jane and John Justin Neuroscience Center offers to treat nervous system diseases?
Assistant: Certainly! The Jane and John Justin Neuroscience Center at Cook Children's offers several innovative programs to treat nervous system diseases. Here are a few examples:

1. Epilepsy Program: Cook Children's is home to one of the largest, most comprehensive pediatric epilepsy programs in the nation. They offer advanced diagnostic techniques, such as video EEG monitoring and long-term EEG monitoring, as well as a wide range of treatment options, including medications, diet therapy, VNS (vagus nerve stimulation), and innovative surgical procedures like robot-assisted minimally invasive laser ablations.

2. Movement Disorders Program: Cook Children's has a dedicated program to help children with movement disorders like cerebral palsy, dystonia, and spasticity. They use a multidisciplinary approach to treatment, including physical and occupational therapy, medication management, and surgery.

3. Stroke Program: The Stroke Program at Cook Children's provides rapid response and coordination of care for children who have experienced a stroke. They have a dedicated Stroke Team that includes neurologists, neurosurgeons, and interventional neuroradiologists to ensure the best possible outcome for each patient.

4. Headache Program: Cook Children's Headache Program provides comprehensive evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment of headaches in children, adolescents, and young adults. The program uses a multidisciplinary approach, including neurology, psychology, and physical therapy.

5. Brain Tumor Program: The Brain Tumor Program at Cook Children's provides highly specialized care for children with brain and spinal cord tumors. They offer advanced diagnostic and treatment options, including minimally invasive surgical techniques, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy.

These are just a few examples of the innovative programs at the Jane and John Justin Neuroscience Center at Cook Children's. They are committed to providing the best possible care for children with nervous system diseases and staying on the cutting edge of research and treatment options.

"Nessa loves colours and she loves discos and when I found out she was losing her sight I went 'I need to do something really special for her'," Ms Williames said.
The family recently heard a diagnosis for Nessa's condition which has been degenerative since the age of about three and resulted in years of "often invasive" testing.
After a full genome sequence, they discovered with both "shock" and "relief" that Nessa had a very rare neurological disorder called infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy.
Ms Williames only knows of two other people in Australia with the condition.
"She was really quite bright. The signature of this disease is children lose everything they had. They gain these milestones then they lose them again," Ms Williames said.
Nessa has the atypical form of the condition, which Ms Williames said meant she was likely to live longer than if she had the classic form, but she was still "on borrowed time".
Last Christmas Nessa started having absent seizures and her family started suspecting her vision was failing.
Then testing revealed optic nerve atrophy, confirming Nessa was losing her eyesight.
Ms Williames said she had dealt with her daughter's condition for 12 years, but the extent of her degeneration made it now "so hard".
"The hardest thing is going into shops now at Christmas because there's nothing I can buy Nessa," she said.
"There's nothing ... That she can get. She can't play with jigsaws, she can't play with toys ... It's horrible."
Ms Williams explained how having INAD meant Nessa could not control her emotions when it came to love and sentiment.
"She can't watch television because she never knows what emotional music coming up. She doesn't know if friends are saying goodbye so that just upsets her so much," she said.
"Virtually the only thing left is love and being happy and oh my gosh she is the most happy child."
The boxes of coloured paper at tomorrow's disco are the product of Nessa's long-term "mission".
"She can't use scissors but what we worked out she can do is rip paper, so for years she has been ripping up little bits of catalogues like confetti for her discos," Ms Williames said.
"She just humbles me so much ... She's just smiling all the time."

INAD can cause a range of symptoms, including delayed development, loss of motor skills, loss of vision, and emotional distress. User: Research. On the surface a conceptually simple task: you ask a question, design a study to test your hypothesis and arrive at a conclusion. All great medical programs focus on research as one of the three pillars of program excellence, along with superior clinical care and education of the next generation of providers. Without research, programs fail to evolve, their care fails to progress and their patients inevitably are the ones that suffer. However, research is no simple task. It takes a team of personnel dedicated to research design, data acquisition, patient safety, data analysis and regulatory compliance. The Jane and John Justin Neurosciences Center at Cook Children's has long been a leader in quality care of nervous system diseases, evidenced by first class programs to treat epilepsy, movement disorders, stroke, headaches, brain tumors and more. Through the support of donors and the dedication of our faculty, our programs have pioneered technologies such as deep brain stimulation for childhood dystonias and robot-assisted minimally invasive laser ablations to treat epilepsy. The Neurosciences Research Endowment, a $30 million fund to support research infrastructure and development, will ensure Cook Children's continues to grow as a leader in neurosciences research, building on our strong foundation of innovative care. Thanks to a generous $15 Million endowment gift from the Dodson Living Trust, Cook Children's will now enhance the Jane and John Justin Neuroscience Center by establishing a dedicated clinical neuroscience research team to expand research efforts; affording our patients access to the most advanced neurological care. For over two decades Clarabele (Pit) Dodson and her late husband Tom have generously supported Cook Children's in our pursuit to make this region one of the healthiest to raise a child. When asked about her support of Cook Children's, Ms. Dodson simply states, "Our children are our future." M. Scott Perry M.D., medical director of Neurology said, "The Dodson Foundation's generous gift is an unprecedented vote of confidence in what Cook Children's Neurosciences can accomplish. They've seen our past successes and believe in our vision for the future of pediatric neurological care. With this support, we can raise the quality of our research to match that of our superior clinical care." The dedicated Neurosciences research staff will work closely with faculty on study design, data analysis and publication of results. Dr. Perry's vision is to increase collaborations with other national and international centers, improving the quality of investigator-initiated studies as well as patient outcomes through this endeavor. This gift marks a turning point in research at Cook Children's and lays a solid foundation for great things to come. This innovative technology allows for a minimally invasive procedure where a small hole is made in the skull and a laser is used to destroy the tissue causing seizures. The procedure is guided by real-time MRI, which allows for precise targeting of the tissue without damaging surrounding healthy tissue. The robot-assisted nature of the procedure allows for even greater precision and enhances patient safety. This treatment option has become a game-changer for patients with epilepsy who may not have responded well to medications or other conventional treatment options. It has also resulted in shorter hospital stays and faster recovery times. The Jane and John Justin Neuroscience Center is one of the leading centers in the country in pioneering the use of this technology for the treatment of epilepsy.

User: How do new advancements in neuroscience impact the field of medicine, and what new treatments are being developed as a result?
Assistant: Advancements in neuroscience have revolutionized the field of medicine, particularly in the diagnosis and treatment of neurological disorders. Here are some ways in which new advancements in neuroscience impact medicine:

1. Understanding the brain better: Neuroscience has led to a better understanding of the underlying mechanisms and pathways that govern brain function. This has led to the development of better diagnostic tests and treatments for neurological disorders.

2. Non-invasive imaging techniques: Advanced imaging techniques like functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), magnetoencephalography (MEG), and positron emission tomography (PET) have made it possible to visualize the living brain in real time. This has helped in identifying neurological disorders early and developing personalized treatment plans.

3. Improved medication: Understanding of the workings of the brain has led to the development of more effective drugs with better precision in targeting specific neurotransmitters and receptors that play a role in the pathophysiology of neurological disorders.

4. Neuromodulation therapies: Advances in neuroscience have opened up new frontiers in neuromodulation therapies. These include deep brain stimulation (DBS), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), which have shown promising results in treating neurological disorders.

5. Brain-machine interfaces (BMIs): BMIs are devices that connect the brain to a computer, enabling patients to control external devices like prosthetic limbs or wheelchairs using their thoughts. BMIs have revolutionized the field of neuroprosthetics, giving people with disabilities new ways to interact with the world around them.

In summary, new advancements in neuroscience have led to a better understanding of the brain's functioning and its role in neurological disorders. This has resulted in the development of new treatments, both pharmacological and non-pharmacological, that have shown promising results in treating neurological disorders.
User: Can you give me an example of a specific neurological disorder that has benefited from advancements in neuroscience?
Assistant: Parkinson's disease is an example of a neurological disorder that has benefited from advancements in neuroscience. 

Parkinson's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder that affects movement and is caused by the loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the brain. Advancements in neuroscience have led to a better understanding of the underlying mechanisms of Parkinson's disease and have resulted in the development of more effective treatments.

One example of a new treatment is deep brain stimulation (DBS), which involves implanting electrodes into specific regions of the brain to deliver electrical impulses that modulate the activity of malfunctioning brain circuits. DBS has been found to be effective in reducing motor symptoms and improving quality of life in patients with Parkinson's disease.

Another example is the development of new medication that can offset the loss of dopamine-producing neurons. One such medication is levodopa, which is converted into dopamine in the brain and can improve motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease. However, ongoing research is still being conducted to improve the safety and efficacy of these medications.

Overall, the advancements in neuroscience have improved our understanding of Parkinson's disease and led to the development of promising new treatments.
User: Can you tell me more about brain-machine interfaces and how they work?
Assistant: Brain-machine interfaces (BMIs) are devices that connect the brain to an external device, such as a computer or a robotic limb, allowing users to control it with their thoughts. There are two main types of BMIs: invasive and non-invasive.

Invasive BMIs involve implanting electrodes directly into the brain to record the activity of individual neurons. The activity is then translated into commands that can control an external device. This type of BMI provides the highest level of control and precision, but it has potential risks associated with brain surgery and the long-term stability of the implants.

Non-invasive BMIs use external sensors that detect brain activity from the scalp, such as electroencephalography (EEG) or magnetoencephalography (MEG), to record the electrical signals produced by groups of neurons. The activity is then analyzed using computer algorithms to decode the user's intended movement or action, which can be used to control an external device. Non-invasive BMIs are less invasive, but they generally provide lower levels of control and precision when compared to invasive BMIs.

To operate a BMI, the user learns to control their brain signals through a process of biofeedback training. This involves receiving feedback about their brain signals, such as visual or auditory cues, that help them learn how to produce specific patterns of brain activity that correspond to different movements or actions. With practice, users can learn to control external devices with their thoughts alone.

BMIs have significant potential to help individuals with disabilities or injuries that limit their ability to move or communicate. For example, BMIs have been used to help individuals with paralysis control robotic limbs or to help individuals with speech impairments communicate through a computer voice synthesizer. BMIs are a promising field of research, and ongoing research aims to refine their accuracy, reliability, and usability.

Assistant: Absolutely! One classic book that comes to mind is "When Pride Still Mattered: A Life of Vince Lombardi" by David Maraniss. It's a biography of the legendary football coach, but it's also a great exploration of the history of the sport and the societal context of the time.
User: That sounds amazing. I'll definitely add it to my list. What about other sports? Are there any good books about, say, basketball or baseball?
Assistant: Oh, yeah! For basketball, I highly recommend "The Book of Basketball" by Bill Simmons. It's a comprehensive history of the sport, covering everything from its early days to the modern era. User: Awesome, I'll check those out. Thanks for the recommendations! I'm excited to dive into some new books and explore the world of sports literature.

Assistant: That sounds like a great idea! What are some other topics you're interested in? Hobbies, history, science, sports?

In addition to live-streaming matches, viewers will be able to watch highlight shows and review programs. Tencent Sports will live-stream all matches and programs across all platforms, including its website, Tencent Video app, Tencent Sports app and Tencent news app.
Tencent’s editorial team will also provide the best clips and programmes to fans, in addition to the live streaming. Their eventual goal is to serve all football fans comprehensively, and bring Europe’s top football matches closer to the fans.

User: Can you provide examples of sportsmanship in different sports, as mentioned in the text? Answer according to: As a Year 6 teacher, I’m sure you can imagine; we’re in the final throws of SATs preparation in my class. Yes there are the obligatory practice papers, but we’ve also enjoyed celebrating Shakespeare’s anniversary and The Queen’s 90th birthday – which also provided great opportunities for writing evidence! Now, this is tricky for me on numerous levels, not least because I’ve only taught them since September and I don’t want to openly criticise previous teachers – regardless of whether they are at the school or have long since departed. So, where to turn for inspiration in answering honestly? The world of sport of course! At the start of the week, watching Ronnie O’Sullivan lose to Barry Hawkins I watched, impressed with how (despite Ronnie putting him under pressure to pull back to level terms) Barry Hawkins admitted a foul; missed by the referee and commentators alike! This let Ronnie in and could have cost Barry the match – it didn’t! Amongst snooker players this is not a rare occurrence, Judd Trump did the same a few days before and I remember Jimmy White doing so in a World Final against Stephen Hendry – unlike Hawkins and Trump, he lost! Or what about football? Paulo Di Canio’s infamous moment of sportsmanship against Everton still lingers in the memory. Alternatively, there’s Robbie Fowler’s moment of honesty against Arsenal – albeit ruined by Jason McAteer! You see, having taught my class to be independent learners (thanks #unhomework!) , they not only spend time voluntarily practicing and reviewing their performance and plugging ‘gaps’, they also want to know more. In doing this, supported by parents, this was an area that seemed to cause a concern – based on a 1 mark question on a practice paper (out of 50, the children having scored 48, 45, 43 and 42 respectively!) Now active to passive voice and vice versa had been a doddle – it improves the writing, clauses – the same, even past continuous tense had been mastered, but this? Clearly, whilst the second acronym may reflect my view, it’s not one to repeat to a class of 10-11 year olds! But, as a council estate boy from the outskirts of London – ‘appy ‘ayes (in Middlesex), I have managed 42 years without worrying about it. In fact, I wonder (if they’re honest) how many colleagues have had to learn/ re-learn the grammar to deliver it to Year 6? My need to be honest prevailed and…, well actually, what would you have done? What if it was your own child asking – would that be different, would they deserve more honesty? If only that would get him to meet the standard expected for a Year 6!

However, she soon realized that the ball was going to land in, and tried to resume play. Stosur stopped too, but by then Azarenka had lost the point. The umpire awarded the point to Stosur, but Azarenka went over to her opponent and told her that she had stopped playing before the shot went in, and therefore the point was hers. - In rugby, in the 2003 Rugby World Cup final between England and Australia, England's fly-half Jonny Wilkinson scored a dramatic drop goal with just seconds left on the clock to give his team a historic victory. However, before he could celebrate with his teammates, he went over to the Australian team and shook hands with every player. This act of sportsmanship was widely praised and remembered as a sign of respect for the vanquished opponents.

- In athletics, in the 2016 Rio Olympics women's 5000m final, American runner Abbey D'Agostino and New Zealand's Nikki Hamblin both fell to the ground after getting tangled up. D'Agostino got back up and started running again, but then saw that Hamblin was still on the ground and appeared injured. Instead of continuing the race, D'Agostino helped Hamblin to her feet and encouraged her to keep going. The two runners then completed the race together, holding hands and crossing the finish line to huge applause from the crowd.

However, when he returned to the game a few minutes later, the Cavaliers fans gave him a standing ovation. Pierce later said that he was touched by the gesture, and that it showed that even in the heat of competition, sportsmanship and respect for opponents could still shine through.

Passage: When Gautam Gambhir’s decision to quit the sport finally came through on Tuesday evening, it was no more than yet another news item shoehorned in the sports pages.
No room for glowing appraisals, as there were more important things at hand from Adelaide where India had been gearing up to start their campaign in the Test series against Australia.
Yes, ‘Gauti,’ as he was known among his teammates, had become somewhat of a passe in Indian cricket.
The interest is likely to centre on his prospective foray into politics rather than the footprint that the angry young man of Indian cricket had left in the game — so what if he was a vital cog in the wheel for the team in all formats from 2007 and 2012 and played a key role in the two World Cup triumphs? May be, he deserved than this.
There is no shortage of common wisdom about ‘timing’ of one’s retirement well — so that once a performer of the highest order can guard himself from getting relegated as an also-ran.
However, the call is not often that easy to make when one is still in his early thirties, the form may be a bit scratchy but the self belief of having enough left in the tank still there.
This was certainly the case with Gambhir, who played his last One-day International way back in 2013 and recalled to play his last Test in 2016 — albeit somewhat fortuitously. All along the years of wilderness, he had been a regular in the domestic scene for Delhi, had a stint with the current Australian coach Justin Langer to work on his game, scored runs with aplomb in the Indian Premier League (IPL) and grew into an undisputed leader for Kolkata Knight Riders after stepping into the shoes of the iconic captain Sourav Ganguly.
It’s a matter of conjecture if his isolation had more to do than just on-field performance — but fact remains that the ICC Test Batsman of the Year for 2009 did not receive an opportunity to sign off on his own terms. No prizes for guessing that it will next be the turn of Yuvraj Singh and Harbhajan Singh — with which four of India’s finest performers since the ‘Fab Five’ will have completed a cycle. Zaheer Khan had timed his exit marginally better in 2015 and then rounding it up with a IPL next season.
There will be polarised opinions on whether the formidable quartet had been right to pursue their dreams of comebacks — with both Yuvraj and Harbhajan clawing back into the national team on odd occasions. The stakes are much higher in the game today when a ‘retired’ tag can immediately put you out of reckoning in the cold, pragmatic world of the IPL franchises, but it will be myopic to think that they had been pushing their careers only for the moolah.
Yuvraj, for one, has gone on record saying that he would wait till the 2019 World Cup before taking a call on his career. Let cricketing logic do it’s job in selection issues, but the Indian board should be a little more proactive in planning the send-off of this golden generation!

User: Can you give more insight into Gautam Gambhir's career and the impact he had on Indian cricket?
Assistant: Yes, Gautam Gambhir was a vital cog in the Indian cricket team from 2007 to 2012 and played a key role in India's two World Cup triumphs. He was widely regarded as one of the best Indian openers of his generation and had the ability to score runs quickly, both in Tests and limited-overs cricket.

Gambhir played 58 Tests, 147 One-day Internationals, and 37 T20 Internationals for India, scoring over 10,000 runs across all formats. He was known for his gutsy performances in crunch situations, as evidenced by his match-winning knocks in the 2007 T20 World Cup final and the 2011 50-over World Cup final.

Apart from his international career, Gambhir was also an accomplished player in domestic cricket, scoring heavily for his home team Delhi and leading Kolkata Knight Riders to two IPL titles in 2012 and 2014.

Overall, Gambhir's impact on Indian cricket was significant, both on and off the field. He was a tough competitor who embodied the never-say-die spirit of the Indian team during his prime, and his performances helped India achieve some of their greatest successes in international cricket.
